newsitem.title: FINLAND: Analysts debate Bank of Finland's next rate move.
newsitem.headline: Analysts debate Bank of Finland's next rate move.

text.p: Finland's central bank said on Monday it would consider tighter monetary policy if inflation accelerated further, but analysts were mixed on whether the remarks pointed to a monetary tightening this year.

Short-term interest rates rose, and the markka jumped against the German mark on the comments, which some economists said marked a shift from the Bank of Finland's earlier assessment that inflation was well under control despite heady economic growth.
"The Bank of Finland clearly indicated that...they feel inflation pressures have become significantly higher," said Esko Torsti, head of market advisory at S-E Banken here.

The Bank of Finland said in a statement with the release of the February, 1997 issue of its quarterly Markka & Talous (Markka and the Economy) publication the risks of accelerating inflation had risen.

It expected underlying 1998 inflation to rise to slightly more than two percent. That compares to a stated monetary policy target for a core inflation rate of no more than around two percent year-on-year.

Though Bank of Finland said "while the current outlook does not portend a change in the stance of monetary policy, an increase in the probability that inflation will exceed the forecasted rate would force the central bank to consider monetary tightening," some economists were revising expectations for a tightening.

"This was the first warning, maybe there will be a second warning, maybe not. But in any case, the time for the next tightening is drawing reasonably close," Torsti said. He said a rate hike was now more likely to come in the third quarter rather than in the final quarter as S-E Banken had forecast as the earliest a tightening would occur.

Kirsi Hokka, chief economist at Handelsbanken Markets Finland, said "I still don't believe that it (a key rate hike) will come before the turn of the year...but that does not mean that a tightening would be ruled out."

The central bank's view that risks of accelerating inflation had increased was a "natural response" to the Paper Workers' Union's announcement last week that it would not join a centralised nation-wide incomes settlement, she said.
Charlotte Kamp, analyst at Den Danske Bank in Copenhagen, said she saw no reason for a Finnish rate hike until 1998 "if the pay talks go smoothly."
But the bank may act pre-emptively as it has before, she added.
Petteri Hirvonen, chief economist at brokerage Davy Protos, said a key rate hike could come in the autumn in connection with the incomes settlement talks, or afterwards.
The markka strengthened in response to prospects of higher rates, and analysts expected further gains.

Though the consensus view has been that the central bank wants to keep the markka near its ERM midpoint, Torsti said "my interpretation is that they are willing to take the risk that the markka's exchange rate against the German mark will stray quite far away, maybe even 10 penni (3.3 percent), from its ERM central parity."
The markka's central parity in the European exchange rate mechanism is 3.04 per mark.
Hokka underlined that monetary policy could also be tightened by allowing the currency to strengthen.
